section.title: The Birth of John and the Benedictus
section.sectionRationale: The promise made at the altar comes true. Elizabeth bears a son, and at his naming Zechariah insists, His name is John, and his long silence is broken. His first words are not complaint but prophecy: the Benedictus, a song blessing the God of Israel who has visited and redeemed His people, raised up a horn of salvation in David's house, and appointed this child to go before the Lord. It is one movement, from a birth that gathers the neighbors' joy to a father's Spirit-filled song of dawning salvation.
section.thesis: God keeps His word: John is born and named as commanded, and the freed tongue of his father blesses the God who has visited and redeemed His people, raising a horn of salvation in David's house and sending the forerunner before the dawning mercy of God.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the birth and naming of John; Zechariah's tongue loosed in praise; the Benedictus blessing the redeeming God; the child who will prepare the way; and John growing in the wilderness.

units.label: The birth and naming of John

verses.text: When the time came for Elizabeth to have her child, she gave birth to a son.
Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown her great mercy, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day, when they came to circumcise the child, they were going to name him after his father Zechariah.
But his mother replied, “No! He shall be called John.”
They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.”
So they made signs to his father to find out what he wanted to name the child.
Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they were all amazed.

units.label: Zechariah's tongue loosed in praise
units.note: what then will this child become

verses.text: Immediately Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak, praising God.
All their neighbors were filled with awe, and people throughout the hill country of Judea were talking about these events.
And all who heard this wondered in their hearts and asked, “What then will this child become?” For the Lord’s hand was with him.

units.label: The Benedictus: the God who redeems
units.note: a horn of salvation in the house of David

verses.text: Then his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied:
“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and {{lytrosis|redeemed}} His people.
He has raised up a {{keras|horn}} of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,
as He spoke through His holy prophets, those of ages past,
salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,
to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant,
the oath He swore to our father Abraham, to grant us
deliverance from hostile hands, that we may serve Him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.

units.label: The child who will prepare the way
units.note: the tender mercy of our God

verses.text: And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him,
to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins,
because of the {{splanchna|tender mercy}} of our God, by which the {{anatole|Dawn}} will visit us from on high,
to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.”

units.label: John grows in the wilderness
units.note: until his public appearance to Israel

verses.text: And the child grew and became strong in spirit; and he lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.

lytrosis.gloss: Redemption, ransoming, deliverance by payment of a price. Zechariah blesses God because He has visited and worked redemption for His people. The word looks back to the exodus and forward to the greater redemption Christ will accomplish.

keras.gloss: Horn, a common biblical image of strength and victory, drawn from the horn of a powerful animal. A horn of salvation in David's house means a mighty Savior-King, fulfilling the promise of a strong deliverer from David's line.

splanchna.gloss: The inward parts, and so deep, gut-level compassion; here the tender mercy of God. It names the warm, heartfelt pity of God that moves Him to visit and save His people, the wellspring of the whole song.

anatole.gloss: The rising, as of the sun or a star, hence dawn or daybreak; the word can also mean a branch or shoot. Applied to Christ, it pictures the sunrise from heaven breaking on a world in darkness, bringing light and the path of peace.

basic.context: Elizabeth gives birth, and her neighbors rejoice at the Lord's mercy. At the boy's circumcision they assume he will be named after his father, but Elizabeth insists on John, and Zechariah, still mute, writes, His name is John. At once his speech returns and he praises God. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesies the Benedictus: blessing the God of Israel who has visited and redeemed His people, raised a horn of salvation in David's house, and remembered His covenant with Abraham. Then he turns to his infant son, who will go before the Lord to prepare His way. John grows up in the wilderness until the day he appears to Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: The naming scene shows obedient faith: Zechariah does exactly what the angel commanded, and his tongue is freed, discipline giving way to praise. The Benedictus, like the Magnificat, is a mosaic of Old Testament promises, so it should be read as the voice of Israel's whole hope finding its answer. The key questions are what God has done in visiting His people and what role this child will play in the dawning salvation.
basic.originalLanguages: Zechariah blesses God who has worked lytrosis, redemption, for His people, raising a keras, a horn, of salvation in David's house. The song springs from the splanchna, the tender mercy, of God, by which the anatole, the Dawn or sunrise from on high, will visit those in darkness.
basic.typology: The horn of salvation from David's house fulfills God's covenant promise of a strong deliverer from David's line. John steps into the role of the prophet who prepares the Lord's way, and the rising Dawn from on high recalls Malachi's sun of righteousness, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.christ: Though the song blesses God the Father, its center is the coming Christ: the horn of salvation, the Lord whose way John prepares, and the Dawn from on high who brings light and peace. John's whole future is to point to Him.
basic.god: God is faithful to His covenant and His oath to Abraham, tender in mercy, mighty to redeem, and the giver of light and peace. He remembers, He visits, and He saves.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 132 promises a horn to sprout for David. Malachi 4 foretells the sun of righteousness rising with healing. Genesis 22 records the oath to Abraham. And Isaiah 9 speaks of light dawning on those in darkness.
basic.oneStory: God visits and redeems, and the forerunner is born to prepare the way. The Benedictus gathers up centuries of promise and announces that the dawn has come: the covenant is kept, salvation is near, and the path of peace is opening for a people long in darkness.

context.literary:
Luke 1:57-80 is the last panel of a carefully built diptych. Chapter 1 pairs two announcements, two pregnancies, two songs and two births, and the two halves are stitched together with matching beats. An angel speaks, a human doubts or believes, a woman is vindicated, a child is named, and a hymn answers. Mary's Magnificat looks back over Israel's history in the past tense. Zechariah's Benedictus does something slightly different: it looks back and forward at once, and then turns to speak to the baby in the second person at verse 76.

The Benedictus falls into two stanzas. Verses 68 to 75 are a single long sentence in the Greek, a chain of infinitives and relative clauses all hanging on the opening blessing. Verses 76 to 79 begin with a fresh 'And you, child' and form the second sentence. The first stanza is about what God has done for Israel, the second is about what this child will do and what the 'Dawn' will do through him. The two halves are bound by the word 'visit,' which opens the first at verse 68 and the last at verse 78, so that the whole song is wrapped in God's coming.

Luke also places the naming scene in a ring. The story begins with Elizabeth's mercy and the neighbors' joy, verses 57 and 58, and ends with the neighbors' question and the child's hidden growth, verses 65 to 66 and 80. Between them is the exchange over the name, where Elizabeth and Zechariah, who cannot have conferred aloud, agree. The 'fear' of the neighbors at verse 65 is the same reaction that met the angel in the temple at verse 12, which tells the reader that a visitation of God, and not merely a happy birth, has occurred.

The final verse is a hinge. It closes the infancy cycle for John and sets him in the wilderness, offstage, until chapter 3. Luke will not mention him again until the word of God comes to him there, Luke 3:2.
context.historical:
The scene is a village in the hill country of Judea, almost certainly near Jerusalem, in the last years of Herod the Great, Luke 1:5. A Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day, as the law of Abraham's covenant required, Genesis 17:12 and Leviticus 12:3. The naming was customarily part of the same occasion, and the neighbors' assumption in verse 59 that the baby would carry his father's name shows how strongly family continuity was felt. Their objection in verse 61 that no relative bears the name John reveals how deliberately God was breaking the pattern: the child's name belonged to the angel's word at Luke 1:13, not to the family tree.

The signs made to Zechariah in verse 62 imply that he was deaf as well as mute. The Greek verb of Luke 1:62 means the neighbors made signs to him, and the writing tablet he asks for is a small wax or wooden board of the ordinary kind. A priest of the course of Abijah, Luke 1:5, he had come home from his service in Jerusalem unable to bless the people, and nine months of silence form the historical backdrop for the release of verse 64.

The content of the Benedictus is thoroughly Jewish in its hopes. 'Salvation from our enemies' and 'from the hand of all who hate us' were not abstract phrases to a people under Roman and Herodian rule. The 'horn' was a familiar picture of strength, drawn from the horns of an ox, and the house of David had not held a throne for roughly six centuries. When Zechariah speaks of serving God 'without fear' he is naming the very thing that foreign domination had made impossible, free and fearless worship in the temple his own service had just left.

The wilderness of verse 80 is probably the thinly settled country of Judea toward the Dead Sea. Luke is not claiming a connection with any particular community there. He is simply preparing a prophet's setting, which Isaiah's promise of a voice in the wilderness had already marked out, Isaiah 40:3.
context.canonical:
The Benedictus is stitched from the Old Testament, and tracing the threads shows how much Luke thinks the whole canon is converging here. The opening blessing, 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,' is the doxology that closes several books of the Psalter, Psalm 41:13, Psalm 72:18 and Psalm 106:48. The 'horn' raised up for David recalls Psalm 132:17, where the Lord says He will make a horn grow for David and has prepared a lamp for His anointed. The oath to Abraham in verses 72 and 73 goes back to Genesis 22:16 to 18, and Micah ends his prophecy with the same pairing of loving devotion to Abraham and the oath sworn to the fathers, Micah 7:20.

The second stanza draws on Isaiah and Malachi. A messenger who will prepare the way before the Lord comes from Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3. The people 'in darkness and in the shadow of death' on whom light dawns are Isaiah 9:2, a text Matthew will quote when Jesus settles in Galilee, Matthew 4:14 to 16. The 'Dawn' from on high touches Malachi 4:2, where the sun of righteousness rises with healing in its wings, and Numbers 24:17, where a star comes out of Jacob.

After the Benedictus the canon keeps the song's three themes in motion. Forgiveness of sins becomes the core of the apostolic message, Acts 10:43 and Acts 13:38. The oath to Abraham is explained by Paul, who reads the promise as given to one seed, Galatians 3:16, and by Hebrews, which says that because God could swear by no one greater He swore by Himself, Hebrews 6:13 to 18. And the 'path of peace' recurs at the angels' song of Luke 2:14, at Jesus' lament over Jerusalem in Luke 19:42, and in the risen Christ's own greeting, Luke 24:36.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is writing for readers who need confidence in what they have been taught, Luke 1:4, and the Benedictus is part of his evidence. He wants them to see that the birth of Jesus was not an unexpected event that the church later dressed in Old Testament language. It was announced, in advance, by Spirit-filled voices who read the Scriptures rightly. Zechariah is a priest who has just been disciplined for unbelief, and Luke lets him be the first person in the Gospel to prophesy the whole shape of salvation. That is itself a lesson in grace: the one who doubted the word now speaks it.

Luke also wants the reader to hear who the song is really about. Zechariah is a father holding a son, yet nearly the entire song is about someone else. The child's role is stated in just two verses, 76 and 77, and it is entirely a role of service: go on before, prepare the way, give knowledge of salvation. By setting John's greatness beside the greater One he serves, Luke prepares the reader for the later exchange in which John says that Jesus must increase, as John 3:30 phrases it, and he must decrease.

Finally, Luke intends to define salvation. In verses 71 and 74 it sounds like national rescue from enemies. In verse 77 it is 'the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins.' The song does not cancel the first hope; it deepens it, showing that the ultimate enemies are guilt, darkness and death, and that fearless service of God, verse 74, is the goal of the rescue and not merely a by-product of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes a miracle of timing and a prophecy; it does not set out rules for naming children, for how long a believer should stay silent, or for how God will deal with doubters. Zechariah's silence in Luke 1:20 was a particular sign for a particular priest, and its removal here is not a promise that every season of doubt ends with a sudden gift of speech. The story does not tell parents to ignore their relatives on naming either, though it does show a household willing to obey a word from God at some social cost.

What does carry across is the pattern of response. When God has spoken, the right answer is to do what He said, as Elizabeth and Zechariah do, and then to praise Him. The first act of the freed tongue is blessing, not argument. The Benedictus also gives believers a way to pray: it starts with God's deeds, goes back to His oaths, and arrives at holy service, which is the order of a healthy Christian worship.

The song's promise of fearless service 'in holiness and righteousness' is a description of what God's rescue is for, and so it also functions as an expectation. Deliverance is not an end in itself. Those who have been brought out of hostile hands are brought into the Lord's own presence, to serve Him all their days, verses 74 and 75.

debates.question: Is the 'visit' of verse 68 already complete, or still to come?

views.label: Already accomplished
views.case: Verse 68 uses past tenses: God 'has visited and redeemed' and 'has raised up' a horn. Since Jesus has not yet been born, some read this as the prophet's way of speaking about a certainty as if it were done, a prophetic perfect. The conception of Jesus in Luke 1:35 has already taken place, so God's saving act has indeed begun.

views.label: Begun and not yet finished
views.case: Others point out that the song looks to a future that is still unfolding. Verse 78 reads 'the Dawn will visit us' in the BSB, and the Greek manuscripts are divided between a past and a future form of that verb. Taken together the song describes a visitation that has started in the child already conceived and will be completed in His ministry, death and return.

debates.bearing: The two views meet in the idea of inaugurated salvation. The Gospel treats the conception, birth and ministry of Jesus as one visit of God, begun here and carried through to the cross and the empty tomb, which is why the crowd at Nain can say in Luke 7:16 that God has visited His people.

debates.question: Who is 'the Lord' that John will go before in verse 76?

views.label: God the Father
views.case: The song begins by blessing 'the Lord, the God of Israel,' and the verses before use 'Lord' for the Father. Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 speak of preparing the way before the LORD, and some hold that Zechariah simply continues the reference to God.

views.label: Jesus, the Lord of Luke 1:43
views.case: Elizabeth has already called Mary 'the mother of my Lord,' Luke 1:43, and Luke applies 'Lord' to Jesus repeatedly. John goes 'before the Lord' and the Gospel immediately shows him preparing the way for Jesus, Luke 3:4 to 6. On this reading the language of Isaiah about the LORD's arrival is being applied to the coming of Christ.

debates.bearing: The best answer is probably both at once. Luke's whole narrative treats the coming of Jesus as the coming of God to His people, so that a forerunner for the one is a forerunner for the other. This is one of the earliest places where the Gospel quietly places Jesus in the identity of the LORD.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the song, eulogetos, 'blessed,' is not the common verb of blessing but the adjective the Septuagint uses for God in the doxologies that close sections of the Psalter, Psalm 41:13, 72:18 and 106:48 in the English numbering. Zechariah is not bestowing a blessing on God. He is declaring that God is the one to be blessed, a statement of what is already true. In the same verse the verb for 'visited,' episkeptomai, carries the sense of looking in on someone to care for them, as one visits the sick. The same family of words stands in the Septuagint of Genesis 50:24, where Joseph tells his brothers that God will surely visit them and bring them out of Egypt. Verse 68 therefore carries an exodus echo before the song has reached the word 'redeemed.'

The clause that opens verse 74 gives the purpose of the rescue with the verb latreuo, 'serve.' It is the verb used in the Greek Old Testament for the worship Israel owes to God, and it is exactly the verb of Exodus 3:12 in the Septuagint, where God tells Moses the sign of the rescue will be that the people will worship Him on the mountain. Luke chooses the word of worship, not the word of labor. Israel is freed for liturgy. The adverb 'without fear,' aphobos, rounds it off, and the two words that follow in verse 75, hosiotes and dikaiosyne, 'holiness and righteousness,' pair devotion to God with right conduct toward people. Paul pairs the same two nouns in his description of the new self in Ephesians 4:24.

The verb for 'prepare' in verse 76, hetoimazo, is the verb Luke uses again in Luke 3:4, where the Isaiah text is quoted, and in Luke 1:17 of making ready a people. It describes the setting up of what is needed in advance, the way a guest room is prepared. John does not create the salvation, he arranges the ground for its arrival.

Verse 77 defines the content of John's preaching with two nouns, gnosis, 'knowledge,' and aphesis, 'forgiveness.' The second is a favorite in Luke and Acts. It is the word for the release of prisoners, which is why Jesus uses it for 'liberty to the captives' in the synagogue at Nazareth, Luke 4:18. Forgiveness here is a release, and the knowledge is not information about salvation but an experienced acquaintance with it.

The phrase 'shadow of death' in verse 79 translates a Greek expression, skia thanatou, that the Septuagint uses for the dark places of Psalm 107:10 and Isaiah 9:2. In Isaiah it is the place where a light dawns. Luke's choice ties the Benedictus to the very verse Matthew will use to describe Jesus' arrival in Galilee.

Finally, verse 80 says the child 'grew' and 'became strong,' using two imperfect tenses, ēuxanen and ekrataiouto, a gradual, ongoing growth. Luke uses the same pair, of Jesus in Luke 2:40, and the parallel is deliberate. The noun anadeixis, 'public appearance,' means a formal showing forth or installation, the way a person is publicly declared to office, which prepares the reader for the moment the word of God comes to John in Luke 3:2.

typology.type: The silent priest and the opened mouth
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah's tongue is tied for a season because he did not believe, and it is released when he obeys by writing the name God gave. A silence that ends in praise is a pattern the Old Testament knows, as when the prophet Ezekiel's speechlessness was lifted at the fall of Jerusalem, Ezekiel 33:22. The type points ahead to the voice of the forerunner, whose own message is the breaking of the silence that had lasted since Malachi. It also anticipates the day when mute tongues are loosed by Christ, Mark 7:35 and Isaiah 35:6. The type falls short because Zechariah's speech is restored for himself; in Christ it is restored for a whole people.

A horn is a strong animal's weapon and a figure for power in the Psalms. God promised to make a horn grow for David, Psalm 132:17, and Hannah sang that He would exalt the horn of His anointed, 1 Samuel 2:10. The line seemed to have been cut down, as Isaiah pictured a shoot from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1. Luke announces that the horn has now been raised, in a child conceived in Mary, a descendant of David by Joseph's line, Luke 1:27. The correspondence is fulfilled but also transformed: the strength is not the sword of an earthly king but the cross, where the enemies defeated are sin and death, Colossians 2:15.

typology.type: The Dawn visiting those in darkness
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah promised light on a people walking in darkness, Isaiah 9:2, and Malachi spoke of a sun of righteousness rising with healing, Malachi 4:2. Zechariah brings both together under a single image, the Dawn from on high. The dawn does not wait for the world to climb toward it; it comes down to those who sit in darkness. The escalation is that Jesus later says of Himself, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and the New Testament closes with Him as the bright morning star, Revelation 22:16. The limit of the type is that a sunrise is a natural event repeated daily, while this Dawn arrives once, in a person, and its light does not set.

typology.type: The forerunner who prepares the way
typology.fulfillment: The role of a messenger sent ahead is as old as the practice of kings sending heralds to level roads before their arrival, and Isaiah uses that picture of the coming of the LORD, Isaiah 40:3. Malachi adds that God will send a messenger and then Elijah, Malachi 3:1 and 4:5. Jesus identifies John as the one of whom this was written, Luke 7:27, and as the Elijah who was to come, Matthew 11:14. John is a type in the sense that his entire ministry is a pointer. The pattern falls short at one point only, and John himself says it, that he is not worthy to untie the sandals of the One who follows, Luke 3:16.

study.christ:
The song blesses the Father, but its centre of gravity is the One whose coming it describes, and the first thing it says about Him is where He comes from. 'In the house of His servant David' makes the horn of salvation a royal descendant, which Gabriel had already said, Luke 1:32 and 33. Zechariah's oath-language ties the Messiah to the covenant with Abraham as well, so that the Christ is both the son of David and the seed of Abraham, the two covenants coming to one person, as Matthew's genealogy begins by saying, Matthew 1:1.

The second thing the song says is how He comes. The image of the Dawn is of a light that arrives from above, from 'on high,' and that rises over people who have been sitting in the dark. The rest of the New Testament takes up the same movement. The Word became flesh and the light shines in the darkness, John 1:5 and 14. Jesus claims it of Himself, John 8:12, and Paul says that God, who said let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6. Zechariah's 'knowledge of salvation' of verse 77 is, in the end, a person to be known.

Third, the song says what He comes to do. John gives the knowledge of forgiveness, but it is Christ who gives the forgiveness itself. In the upper room He speaks of His blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins, Matthew 26:28, and in the final chapter of Luke He tells the disciples that repentance and forgiveness of sins would be preached in His name to all nations, Luke 24:47. The pairing of 'tender mercy' and 'visit' becomes the cross, in which the mercy of God takes the form of a body given.

Fourth, the song says where He leads. Feet are guided into 'the path of peace,' and Christ is Himself the way, John 14:6, who makes peace by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20, and who speaks the word of peace to His disciples after the resurrection, Luke 24:36.

A caution keeps this honest. Zechariah did not know the details of the cross, and he would have heard his own song as the hope of Israel's rescue. What Luke asks the reader to see is that the rescue he sang about is larger than he imagined, and that his words, spoken under the Spirit, say more than he fully grasped, the way the prophets searched to understand the time to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing, 1 Peter 1:10 to 11.
study.god:
The Benedictus is a song about a God who acts and a God who remembers, and it is built around those two verbs. 'Remember' in verse 72 does not mean that God had forgotten. In Scripture it is the word for God acting on what He has pledged, as when He remembered Noah and the waters receded, Genesis 8:1, and when He heard the groaning of Israel and remembered His covenant, Exodus 2:24. The song shows a God who treats an old promise as binding and who has not let four centuries of prophetic silence loosen it.

It shows a God whose power and mercy work together. The horn is a picture of strength, and the 'tender mercy' of verse 78 is a picture of affection. The word for tender mercy in the Greek is built on the word for a person's inward parts, the seat of deep compassion, and it describes what moves the Father toward His people. The power that raises a horn and the compassion that sends a Dawn do not compete. The God who rescues from enemies is the same God whose mercy begins the rescue.

It shows a God who rescues for a purpose. He frees in order to be served, and the service is described in the language of holiness and righteousness 'before Him,' verse 75. Redemption is therefore not escape from God but arrival at Him. The doctrine of salvation in these verses cannot be reduced to rescue from a danger. It includes a destination, a life lived in His sight.

It shows a God who is faithful across generations. He swears to Abraham, speaks through prophets 'of ages past,' verse 70, and fulfils in a child in the hill country of Judea. The point is that His word has a history and a unity, and the God of the oath is the God of the visit.

It shows a God who is Trinitarian in the shape of His working, though the word does not appear. The Lord is blessed, the Spirit fills the prophet, verse 67, and the Dawn visits from on high, so that Father, Spirit and Son stand in the same sentence. The conception that Luke recorded earlier, by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, Luke 1:35, has produced this chain of divine acts.

For worship, the song teaches the order of praise. Begin by blessing God for what He has done, go back to what He has promised, and then end in a life of unafraid devotion. The person who prays the Benedictus learns that gratitude and obedience are two sides of the same confidence in a God who keeps His word.

crossReferences.note: The Lord swears an oath to David and promises that a horn will grow for him and a lamp be prepared for His anointed. Zechariah's phrase 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David' reads like a reply to this psalm. The oath is kept, but through a child the psalmist could not have named.

After Abraham is willing to offer Isaac, God swears by Himself that all nations will be blessed through his offspring. Verses 72 and 73 of the Benedictus call this 'the oath He swore to our father Abraham.' Luke wants us to hear that the birth of Jesus is the unfolding of this covenant and not a new beginning.

The prophet ends with praise of a God who pardons iniquity, delights in loving devotion and shows faithfulness to Jacob as He swore to the fathers. The conjunction of pardon, mercy and the oath to the fathers is exactly the combination of Luke 1:72 and 77. The final word of the Old Testament's prophetic books of repentance is the first word of Zechariah's song.

A voice calls for the way of the LORD to be prepared in the wilderness. Luke quotes this in full at Luke 3:4 to 6 for John's ministry, and here Zechariah anticipates it in verse 76. The wilderness of verse 80 is where this voice is trained.

God promises to send a messenger to prepare the way before Him, and then the Lord whom the people seek will suddenly come to His temple. Luke 1:76 follows the same order: a forerunner, then the Lord. The temple setting of the story, where Zechariah served, makes the allusion fit.

For those who fear God's name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings. The Dawn from on high of Luke 1:78 shares the image of a rising light that heals. Malachi sets it at the close of the Old Testament, and Zechariah sets it at the opening of the New.

Light dawns on the people walking in darkness and on those living in the land of the shadow of death. Luke 1:79 applies that language to the effects of the Dawn. Matthew quotes the same verse of Jesus' move to Galilee in Matthew 4:14 to 16, so both Gospels read it as the dawn of Christ.

Gabriel's announcement to Zechariah already describes John as one who will turn many to the Lord, go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah, and make ready a people prepared. The Benedictus repeats these themes and gives the prophecy a voice. The naming in verse 60 and 63 is the obedience Gabriel asked for at Luke 1:13.

God tells Moses that the sign of the deliverance from Egypt will be worship on the mountain. The Septuagint of this verse uses the same verb Zechariah uses in Luke 1:74 for serving God. The Benedictus hears the exodus pattern again: rescue is for worship, and freedom is for service.

Samuel's growth is described in a sentence much like Luke 1:80 and 2:40, which also say a boy grew and was strong. Luke is quietly setting John, and later Jesus, in the line of Samuel, a child dedicated to God whose coming marked a turn in Israel's story.

Paul announces forgiveness of sins through Jesus to the synagogue at Antioch. This is the apostolic fulfillment of the knowledge Zechariah says John will give. What the Benedictus puts in the future, the gospel preached in Acts delivers.

study.oneStory:
The Benedictus is a point where the whole Bible's story is gathered into a few lines. It begins in the covenant with Abraham, when God swore to bless all nations through his offspring, Genesis 22:18, and it passes through David, when the promise of a throne was added, 2 Samuel 7:12 and 13. It remembers the exodus in its vocabulary of redemption and worship, and it remembers the prophets who spoke of darkness and of a coming light. It also remembers the long dark that followed the exile, when the people were back in the land but under foreign rule and the prophetic voice had gone quiet.

What it answers from before is the question of whether God had forgotten. The people of Zechariah's day had waited for centuries, and the temple where he served was a standing reminder of promises not yet kept. Zechariah's song says that nothing was forgotten. 'He has visited and redeemed His people' is the answer to the cry of the exiles in Psalm 74 and Lamentations 5.

What it sets up is the whole Gospel. John's ministry in the wilderness begins in Luke 3, the child Mary is carrying will be born in Luke 2, and the knowledge of forgiveness will be given on the cross. The shadow of death in verse 79 anticipates the actual shadow of the tomb, and the guided feet are the path that Jesus will walk toward Jerusalem. The song thus provides a map for Luke's entire Gospel.

It also looks beyond Luke to the church. The service 'without fear' of verse 74 is what the church does when she worships in the Spirit, and the peace of verse 79 is the peace that Christ gave to His disciples and leaves with the church, John 14:27.

It ends in the new creation. The Dawn from on high is the light that will make the sun unnecessary, for in the new Jerusalem the Lord God will give light, and there will be no more night, Revelation 22:5. The shadow of death will be gone, the enemies defeated, and God's people will serve Him, Revelation 22:3, exactly as Zechariah sang, in holiness and righteousness, without fear, all their days.

sermon.title: Benedictus
sermon.why: Begg walks through Zechariah's prophecy in Luke 1:67-79, focusing on the source, reality, and purpose of God's promised salvation, how His mercy brings light into darkened hearts, forgiveness of sins, and true peace. A faithful, expository handling of the Benedictus at the center of this movement.

quiz.q: Why were the neighbors surprised at the naming of the child?

options.text: Because both parents insisted on John, though no relative bore that name.
options.note: Verses 60 to 63 show the surprise that they broke with family custom to obey the angel's command.

options.text: Because Elizabeth wanted to name him John rather than Zechariah.
options.note: True, but the fuller surprise was that no relative had the name and Zechariah agreed by writing.

options.text: Because they thought the child should have no name at all.
options.note: They intended to name him after his father; the issue was the specific name John.

options.text: Because John was a forbidden name in Israel.
options.note: The name was not forbidden; it simply was not in the family.

quiz.q: What happened when Zechariah wrote, His name is John?

options.text: His mouth was opened and his tongue released, and he began praising God.
options.note: Verse 64 records his speech restored the moment he obeyed.

options.text: The neighbors were all amazed at what had happened.
options.note: They were amazed, but the central event was Zechariah's speech returning as he praised God.

options.text: He remained silent for several more days.
options.note: His silence ended immediately, not later.

options.text: The child began to speak instead.
options.note: It was Zechariah, not the infant, whose speech was restored.

quiz.q: What does Zechariah bless God for in the Benedictus?

options.text: God has visited and redeemed His people, raising a horn of salvation in David's house.
options.note: Verses 68 and 69 are the heart of the song's blessing.

options.text: God has remembered His covenant and oath to Abraham.
options.note: True and part of the song, but the opening blessing centers on the redemption and the horn of salvation.

options.text: God has given Zechariah his voice back.
options.note: That prompted his praise, but the song blesses God for redeeming His people, not merely for the personal sign.

options.text: God has destroyed the Roman Empire.
options.note: The song speaks of salvation and forgiveness, not the overthrow of Rome.

quiz.q: What did Zechariah say his son John would do?

options.text: Go before the Lord to prepare His way and give His people the knowledge of salvation.
options.note: Verses 76 and 77 define John's mission as the forerunner.

options.text: Become a prophet of the Most High.
options.note: True, John is called a prophet, but his defining task was to prepare the Lord's way.

options.text: Reign as king over Israel.
options.note: John prepares the way for the King; he is not the King himself.

options.text: Serve as high priest in the temple.
options.note: John's calling was prophetic preparation, not the high priesthood.

quiz.q: How does the Benedictus picture the coming of the Savior?

options.text: As the Dawn from on high, shining on those in darkness and guiding their feet into peace.
options.note: Verses 78 and 79 use the image of sunrise breaking on the darkness.

options.text: As the tender mercy of God visiting His people.
options.note: True and stated, but the vivid picture is the Dawn rising to bring light and peace.

options.text: As a mighty army driving out Israel's foes.
options.note: The salvation is centered on forgiveness and peace, not a military campaign.

options.text: As a distant hope that may never arrive.
options.note: The song announces the dawn as breaking now; the hope is arriving, not fading.

questions: Zechariah's obedience, writing His name is John, freed his tongue for praise. Where might a simple act of obedience open the way to renewed joy in God for you?
The neighbors asked, What then will this child become? How does it steady you to know that the Lord's hand is at work shaping lives long before we see the outcome?
The Benedictus roots its confidence in a covenant God who remembers His promises. Which promise of God do you most need to remember today?
Zechariah names forgiveness of sins as the heart of salvation. How does keeping forgiveness central guard you from settling for smaller rescues than God offers?
Christ comes as the Dawn to those in darkness and the shadow of death. Where do you long for His light, and how can you walk toward the path of peace this week?

translationNotes.note: A horn of salvation uses the Old Testament image of a horn as a symbol of strength and victory; in David's house it means a mighty deliverer-King, echoing Psalm 132:17.

The Dawn renders a Greek word for the rising of the sun or a star; the BSB footnote gives the alternatives the Morning Light or the Sunrise. The word can also mean a branch, but the context of shining light favors the sunrise.
Became strong in spirit is noted by the source as read in some manuscripts as became strong in the Spirit; either way it marks God's hand preparing John for his prophetic calling.
